input: The pump affinity laws are a set of extremely useful relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its rotational speed is varied, and they are widely used by engineers who need to predict what a pump will do at a speed different from the one at which it was originally tested. In essence, the laws consist of three simple proportionalities. The flow delivered by the pump varies in direct proportion to the speed, so that if the speed is increased, the flow increases in exactly the same ratio. The head produced by the pump varies with the square of the speed, meaning that a change in speed has a considerably more pronounced effect on the head than it does on the flow. The power absorbed by the pump varies with the cube of the speed, which means that the effect on power is more dramatic still. A simple worked check helps to bring this point home: if the speed of the pump is doubled, the power does not merely double in line with the flow; because the power follows the cube of the speed, doubling the speed actually multiplies the power by 8. This is a striking result, and it underlines why even relatively modest increases in pump speed can have surprisingly large consequences for the power that has to be supplied.
target: Pump speed changes move flow, head, and power by fixed proportions, and the affinity laws state the three proportions for a centrifugal pump run at varying speed. Flow varies in direct proportion to speed: at twice the speed the same pump delivers twice the flow, and at half the speed half the flow. Head varies with the square of the speed, so a doubling of speed multiplies the head by the square of the doubling, a steeper response than the flow gives to the same change. Power varies with the cube of the speed, and the cube makes power the most speed-sensitive of the three quantities. The cube is not an accident of the set: power is built from flow and head together, since the pump does work on the flow it delivers against the head it raises, and a quantity formed from the other two carries the speed factors of both and a further factor of its own. A worked check fixes the size of the power effect. Doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8, the cube of the doubling applied to the power at the original speed. Flow and head from the same change grow by the doubling itself and by its square, and neither grows as fast as the power. Each proportion links corresponding operating points of the one pump: the impeller, the casing, and the liquid stay unchanged, and only the speed moves. Read that way, the laws answer a practical question directly. The duty of a known pump at a new speed follows from the duty already measured at a tested speed, with the power term setting the cost of any speed increase.
